planting.note: Set dormant bare-root crowns into well-worked, well-drained soil in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, positioning the crown right at the soil surface so it is neither buried nor left exposed.

directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring with the crown level with the soil surface, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and pinch off the first season's blossoms so the plants put their energy into establishing strong roots and crowns before fruiting heavily the following year. Honeoye was bred at Cornell University's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station and released in the late 1970s, and it became a mainstay June-bearing variety across the colder parts of the Northeast, upper Midwest, and eastern Canada because of its outstanding winter hardiness and dependable, concentrated early-season crop. The berries are large, glossy bright red, and firm, with a bold, tangy-sweet flavor that many growers describe as more assertive than milder modern varieties, and the plants send out runners vigorously to fill in a matted row within a season or two. Honeoye ripens early to midseason and is frequently planted alongside later-fruiting varieties to stretch the harvest window in home gardens and pick-your-own plantings.

planting.note: Set dormant crowns in early spring at the correct planting depth, with the crown level with the soil surface, into a sunny bed amended with compost so the roots can establish before the summer heat arrives.

directions: Set dormant crowns in early spring with the crown at soil level in a sunny, well-drained bed, and remove the runners during the first season if a larger single-crown hill is preferred over a spreading matted row. Sparkle was released in the late 1940s and went on to become the benchmark late-season, high-flavor strawberry for home gardeners across the northeastern and midwestern United States for decades. The berries are medium-sized and comparatively soft-fleshed, ripening at the tail end of the June-bearing season, with an intensely aromatic, old-fashioned strawberry flavor that many gardeners still seek out for fresh eating and preserves. Although firmer, more disease-resistant modern cultivars have largely displaced it from commercial fields, Sparkle remains popular with heirloom growers who prioritize flavor over shipping durability.

planting.note: Set dormant crowns into well-drained, fertile soil in early spring, spacing plants to allow the vigorous runners room to fill in the row, and irrigate during establishment even though the variety tolerates drier soil once rooted.

directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring with the crown even with the soil line, in full sun and well-drained soil, and remove first-year blossoms to build a stronger root system before the main fruiting season. Surecrop was developed by USDA breeders and released in the early 1950s, and it earned its name from an unusually broad range of climate adaptability, performing reliably from the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest into the upper South at a time when most varieties were narrowly suited to a single region. The berries are large, firm, and slightly tart, ripening mid-season, and the plants show strong resistance to red stele root rot and Verticillium wilt along with better-than-average drought tolerance for a June-bearer. Because of this combination of toughness and adaptability, Surecrop was widely planted for decades and used as breeding stock in numerous later strawberry-improvement programs.

planting.note: Set dormant crowns in early spring with the crown level to the soil surface in raised beds or well-drained rows, since Darselect performs best where soggy roots and standing water are not a concern.

directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring at soil level in fertile, well-drained ground, and mulch with straw to keep the large fruit clean and off the soil surface. Darselect was bred in France in the 1990s and quickly became a leading commercial and market-garden variety across western Europe before gaining a following among Mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest growers in North America. The berries are notably large, elongated-conical, and deep glossy red, with dense, firm flesh and a rich, well-balanced sweet flavor that holds up better in storage than many other June-bearing types. It ripens midseason and is often favored by growers who sell at farmers markets because the fruit's size and firmness make for an especially attractive display basket.

common_name: Mara des Bois Strawberry (French Day-Neutral Wild-Flavored Hybrid)

planting.note: Set dormant crowns in early spring with the crown at soil level, and pinch off blossoms for the first several weeks after planting to help day-neutral plants establish before they begin their extended fruiting cycle.

directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring in loose, well-drained soil, and remove flowers for the first few weeks to allow the compact, day-neutral plants to establish a strong root system before continuous fruiting begins through summer and into fall. Mara des Bois was developed in France in the early 1990s by combining garden strawberry lines with genetics from the wild alpine strawberry, giving it a fruity, perfumed aroma reminiscent of wild strawberries that sets it apart from typical supermarket varieties. The berries are small to medium, soft, and highly aromatic rather than large and firm, which makes them a favorite of chefs and farmers-market growers but less suited to long-distance shipping. Because it is day-neutral, Mara des Bois produces a steady trickle of fruit from late spring through fall frost rather than one concentrated June crop.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart; fruiting begins on second-year canes, ripening in the mid-season window.

directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and cut new canes back after their first season to encourage strong lateral branching for the following year's crop. Eldorado was discovered as a chance seedling in Ohio in the early twentieth century and went on to become one of the most widely planted home-garden blackberries in the eastern and midwestern United States for much of the century, valued above all for its reliable cold hardiness and productivity without needing a second variety for pollination. The berries are medium-sized, glossy black, sweet, and nearly seedless-tasting compared to many older thorny types, ripening over a fairly long midseason picking window. Eldorado's erect, self-supporting thorny canes tolerate harsh winters better than many later thornless introductions, which is why it persisted in northern gardens long after flashier commercial varieties came and went.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early to mid-spring, spacing 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart on a support wire; fruiting occurs on second-year canes, ripening mid-to-late season.

directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and train the vigorous, self-supporting canes onto a wire trellis to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. Darrow was developed by USDA breeders and released in the late 1950s, named in honor of the noted small-fruit breeder George M. Darrow, and it was bred specifically for cold hardiness beyond what most erect blackberries of the era could tolerate. The berries are large, firm, glossy black, and tart-sweet, produced in heavy clusters over a mid-to-late season harvest window that extends the bramble season after earlier varieties finish. Its thorny, upright canes and strong winter hardiness have kept it in cultivation as a dependable choice for northern growers who need a blackberry that survives cold winters without cane dieback.

common_name: Hull Thornless Blackberry (USDA Semi-Erect Thornless Bramble)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 4-6 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart, and trellis the semi-erect canes since they arch and sprawl without support.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile soil and tie the semi-erect, arching canes to a two-wire trellis to keep fruit clusters accessible and off the ground. Hull Thornless was developed by USDA-ARS breeders at Beltsville, Maryland and released in the early 1980s as part of a program aimed at combining the thornless trait with better cold tolerance and fruit quality than earlier thornless releases. The berries are medium-to-large, glossy black, and notably sweeter than many of its thornless predecessors, ripening over a fairly long midseason window with good yields once the semi-erect canes are established. Because it tolerates cooler winters better than many thornless trailing types, Hull Thornless became a popular home-garden choice for growers who wanted thornless canes without moving to a warmer climate zone.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

common_name: Doyle's Thornless Blackberry (Vigorous Trailing Thornless Bramble)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 10 feet apart to accommodate exceptionally vigorous, sprawling growth, and provide a sturdy trellis from the start.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained soil and train the long, trailing, thornless canes onto a sturdy multi-wire trellis, since this cultivar's vigor can overwhelm a light support structure within a couple of seasons. Doyle's Thornless was developed and patented by an amateur grower in Illinois and marketed directly to home gardeners rather than released through a university breeding program, and it became known for extremely heavy per-plant yields once established, with growers regularly reporting a single mature plant can produce many gallons of fruit. The berries are medium-to-large, sweet-tart, and hold their shape well for fresh eating, freezing, or preserving, ripening over an extended midseason window. It is self-fertile, though many growers plant more than one to maximize the already generous yields typical of the variety.

common_name: Black Butte Blackberry (Oregon State Extra-Large-Fruited Bramble)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring, spacing 5-8 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart, and trellis the long trailing canes on a two-wire system typical of Pacific Northwest bramble production.

directions: Plant dormant canes in well-drained, fertile soil and train the trailing, thorny canes onto a trellis, pruning out fruited floricanes each year after harvest to keep new primocanes productive. Black Butte was released by the Oregon State University blackberry breeding program in the 1980s and is best known among Pacific Northwest growers for producing exceptionally large fruit, with individual berries often noticeably bigger than those of Marionberry or most other trailing types. The berries ripen early in the trailing-blackberry season, are glossy black with good flavor, and their large size makes hand-picking notably faster than with smaller-fruited varieties. Because the canes are thorny and quite vigorous, Black Butte requires the same sturdy trellising and winter pruning used for other trailing blackberries grown in maritime climates.
